@Polymarket now prices on-demand compute for @nvidia H100s, B200s, and B300s, out to 2028. More chips and terms soon. http://polymarket.com/compute

$HPE CEO: "We expect supply of memory, NAND, and many other critical components to remain constrained to at least H2 2028."

$DELL Vice Chairman: "there’s nothing that suggests that we're going to see price declines in enterprise NAND and DRAM for servers."

JP Morgan note: 

- Per OpenRouter, overall token spend continued to increase (+8% M/M growth), while volume pricing declined -39% M/M. 

- A100 GPU prices increased, H100 and B200 prices also continued to increase M/M

- DRAM price gains moderated, while NAND spot declined. 

On the latter part, I covered China selling inventory on NAND/eSSD spot markets. This was procurement delays around $NVDA GPUs/DRAM shortages, demand to re-accelerate after component arrive. (source Phison CEO)

Enterprise NAND pricing might see different rates than spot markets, as seen with Dell Chairman comments. 

TLDR: 
- Token spend continues to grow despite users shifting to cheaper Chinese models
- Bullish comments on DRAM duration (also seen with $AMBA earnings), but consumer demand weakening
- Compute pricing continues to increase in November
-  More nuanced for NAND, weakness in near term NAND spot markets (with expected rebound after GPUs/DRAM/components arrive), enterprise NAND markets seem resilient.

as i reflect over the past few weeks, i have to admit this is becoming psychologically the toughest bitcoin cycle yet for me, and ive had the pleasure (pain) to live them all-

in an environment where every asset correlated to the downside in a multi-sigma fashion, this would have been a historically important moment to observe bitcoin on a differentiated return path

in fact, one could even argue so much of the bitcoin thesis was in play - the world is literally on fire with both institutional trust at an all time low and surveillance ambitions at all time high, and on top of that we have potentially a real cryptographic risk that would basically blow up the world as we know it for which one could presumably imagine bitcoin offers a distinctly variant though perhaps practically imperfect path. as i reflect on the past fifteen years, im not sure if there will be a more ideal set up than today for people to believe bitcoin can be useful

and yet because bitcoin is not delivering an orthogonal outcome currently, while other assets are simultaneously becoming "more attractive" the temptation to rotate for a better opportunity in terms of cost of capital is incredibly tempting. as an investor, i understand this so deeply. and maybe for the first time, i have found it a lot harder to understand what catalyst to await for. fed policy? i can think of plenty other assets that will run as fast as i need with far less basis risk. sovereign adoption? it looks like the white house is busier buying stakes in US companies. institutional adoption in a post ETF world? not going to work if it compounds at 9% with 40% realized volatility over 3 years. in the past, exchange/business failures were digestible because you knew they were technical in nature that would ultimately resolve itself as long as the asset is not impaired. but what happens if people start to think the asset is impaired?

the honest answer is that an asset is only impaired when it can no longer do what it promised, and it can be trying to remind yourself that nothing bitcoin promised has broken. the truth is that bitcoin never promised a price, a correlation, or a catalyst as much as we would like it to. instead, what it promised is an exit: a supply no one can inflate, settlement no one can censor, and ownership no one can revoke, so that in a world where more and more is granted rather than owned, there is still one thing you can hold without anyone's permission. that exit is still intact today. an exit isn't worth less just because nobody is using it yet, for its value comes from the fact that it's there when everything else locks. so if anything is impaired right now, perhaps it's our patience, which is perhaps the entire ordeal of knowing the price of owning an exit before you need one. its not a satisfying answer, but it doesnt mean its not true

and so its possible we have to hedge for the reality that the world is going to get so much more insane than we know it. tail risks previously unfathomable might materialize. imagine a cyber crisis so severe where the open internet is fundamentally altered in ways we cant yet describe. imagine tail risks where the need to return to things "off-line" become a way of life because the government is infringing upon every right you seek, in privacy and in speech. imagine a world of total wealth extraction via taxation, total labor extraction via automation, total privacy extraction via surveillance. im not really sure if i want to live in that world, and im not sure what kind of financial system will emerge in that world. but in such a dire state, which we increasingly appear to tread towards, it feels to me that the ultimate bitcoin case comes down to one thing: it proves that an exit yet still might exist. and exit ramps by nature are small little holes that cant fit everyone when it becomes consensus

so yes i think its worth holding onto that call option and sometimes yes it can be just that simple

As you guys know I only talk about a specific trade once in a blue moon, but I'm heavily convicted on a Risk/Reward setup here so will share.

NFA, this is just my own thoughts. 

For the past few months I have been doing a deep dive into finding the best ways to invest into the AI trade as it continues to transform the economy. 

Have looked extensively at the range of both public and private opportunities. I think there will be very good high yield opportunities on the privates side that can be done at size, and will look to source these and possibly bring them onchain. 

But in the meantime with the recent huge dislocations in prices, I think the greatest R/R opportunity is on the public side, specifically in @nebiusai $NBIS. 

At the time of this post its at $76-77, anything under $80 with a first target of ~$120 feels like one of the best +50% setups I have seen that can be done in size in a very long time. 

The funding of the AI capex buildout has understandably shaken the market up, as the circular economics are sometimes hard to untangle properly. This combined with Nebius having a delay on one of their sites took the wind out of the stock, which was trading at $160 just a couple weeks ago.

I can write an entire book as a thesis but to keep it very short- There are several advantages Nebius has that made me choose it for this trade:

-The balance sheet is extremely robust for a neocloud and their conservative fiscal approach will help them survive this liquidity airgap.
-Their technical ability on delivering capacity and operating it is extremely high, making them a preferred partners of the major players like NVIDIA, Databrick etc. 
-This also has allowed them to develop scalable business lines like their asset-light model where someone else funds the buildout. The Asset-Light model is already generating huge returns and is underpriced for now as it isn't marked as 'ARR'.
-They have other great assets on the Balance sheet including a very valuable 25% stake in Clickhouse that create even more surface area for things to go well.

There's a lot more for those who want to research more deeply- And while anything is possible in these crazy times, in my estimation this R/R sits at the highest point of  'AI Capex Mountain' -- if the floodwater is going to reach that high then the entire AI sector is cooked anyway.

Timing wise for the 50+% bounce, at this point for it to happen quickly will likely require a liquidity injection of some sort. I don't think we are too far from something like that being needed, though of course it might mean things get worse before they get better so I wouldn't have leverage on at this time. 

Within 6 months I am expecting this to trade a LOT higher and am personally positioning accordingly. Sharing for entertainment purposes only, I know most of us already are deployed and not much in cash so stay safe out there.

Current LLM meta feels special.

Gemini 4 Neon and Opus 5.5 are excellent, despite not being flagship models.

Neon is particularly surprising: up until this point Gemini models have always felt benchmaxxed and unusable for real work.

But Neon is great. I like its writing, it follows scope and instructions well, and its judgment (e.g. the recommendations it offers) is sound. 

It's the kind of model that you can ramble into and it will accurately derive your intent.

I don't get tired of using Neon, and the usual fog that I get after a long period of reading LLM outputs isn't there.

The usage limits for both Claude and Gemini subscriptions are also very generous.

It feels like nearly unlimited intelligence.

I'm using Opus 5.5 and 4 Neon as daily drivers. I like running them independently, but also getting them to work in parallel and check each other's work etc. This is both worthwhile and affordable given the current usage limits.

I'll still loop in Fable 5.2 for hard architectural work or to lift the fog when Neon/Opus get stuck in review loops, but this is rare. They tend to just get the job done.

This is a big change from just a few months ago, where it felt like if you weren't using the bigger/smartest models, you were missing out and were gonna get some dog shit outputs.

Very cool. Would recommend you give these models a spin.

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.

Blog: https://lucidcomputing.ai/blog/introducing-inference-proofs
Platform: https://inferenceproofs.ai
Code: https://github.com/ai-verification-observatory/inference-proofs

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

Yet every time some non-Bitcoiner argues this is all they talk about lol. They do so because from first principles they have come to realise that every other argument against Bitcoin is proving not viable and it's the only thing that's "in the future" that they can knock.

People get stuck on this idea of "bitcoin cant double every 4 yrs to keep incentives for miners and wont be able to rely on fees in decades ahead"

1)You are thinking in fiat terms - there is no reason why it cant nominally on a fiat denominator although it does not need to
2)When fiat becomes increasingly worthless like in many countries the Bitcoin chart is parabolic on parabolic in that currency - the issue is even thinking from fiat view for security long term
3)Long term when your currency goes through very high inflation you are just going to want the Bitcoin - as a thought experiment how much Burmese kiat are you willing to sell Bitcoin for?
4)Bitcoin has gone through multiple 70% declines and had no issues as hashrate readjusts 
5)Miners will continue to search and find more effective ways to mine from equipment to energy costs ie Moores Law
6)In gaining adoption and usage across multiple layers in the long term there is various ways that an increase in fees will also come to bare and a purely fee based incentine is not for over 100 yrs

You cannot understand Bitcoin and think it has a security issue - it goes hand and hand with the premise of Bitcoin - "Bitcoin has a security issues" just means "I dont believe in Bitcoin"

So if you own Bitcoin but believe there is a security issue you need to reduce your exposure because it means you only see the speculation of it and large downside volatility will haunt you as you wont be able to face your thinking based on logic but emotion

From first principles what Bitcoin needs over time is more hash rate - people mistakenly think in the derivative of this by saying “Bitcoin needs to double every 4 years for the security incentive”

That’s a false premise and two different things

Firstly there are multiple reasons hash rate can increase:

-More efficient equipment

-Finding cheaper sources of energy

-Incentives to acquire Bitcoin outside of just market buying

Second hash rate adjusts over time to manage incentives - the same way higher interest rates incentivise demand for Treasuries. A drop in hash rate invites miners who are profitable at different thresholds to come online

Third Bitcoin doesn’t need to double from its previous ATH every 4 years. What it needs is a general upward trend that reflects the cost of energy/mining - which is currently thought in fiat generally USD but not always the case - Reread this point - Reflects cost of energy over time not the fiat quote.

Example: When Bitcoin hit 69k the avg mining cost in USD was ~22k. Four years later post-halving 44k would still be profitable for those same miners had nothing changed and that’s just the average. Some miners have lower, some higher than average and this is not static but a constant motion

If you look at mining cost trends they’ve steadily doubled every four years in USD anyway and even though that’s not required (as mentioned in the points above) it kills the argument and shows a large flaw in the "well it hasnt doubled since 69k" - those miners just got to make a tonne more at that arbitrage but nonetheless profitable and its times like that like the volatility in markets for normal buyers that allows miners to make risk adjusted returns 

And finally, when price rips 3-4x above the avg mining cost, miners sell or bring more rigs online to rebalance and its the short term speculators who are impacted. On the flip side when China banned mining and hash rate dropped, it opened the door for new growth elsewhere and within a year, the hash rate was higher than ever.

One of my favourite things about Bitcoin which is not discussed in most Bitcoin circles as much is this equilibrium function which works on many levels but particularly

1)A shared ethical basis for money where no participant acquires money at a preferential rate risk adjusted
2)That without talking about fiat what its done is tie itself to energy/hardware - hence just the random fiat quote is not the basis for security

If and when the quote is BTC itself (although also does not need to be the case) people will just want BTC because its BTC -  it will be acquired as the end goal it will be like us thinking now about if we could mine USD.
This does not work with gold because even if the quote is in gold - noone can take gold for goods and services due to divisibility and portability issues and needs to then be once removed via some sort of issued paper.

There are many ways to discuss this topic and have never been bothered to as Ive thought this was base level bitcoin understanding but ive figured that with the number of people talking about security cost in the Bitcoin skeptic camps its worth sharing to help increase understanding.
This is the same as when I didnt tweet about investing but then realised basic concepts like "starting from view you could be wrong" was game changing for lot of people.

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
OpenAI has posted their own VP ≠ VNP proof in response to Anthropic's, and says their result 'was obtained on November 6, 2026.' Two weeks ago. The ETH papers were also released in an similar oneupmanship fashion. As with Anthropic's result, no name on the paper (my guess is this was GPT-Aeon). Also like Anthropic: no announcement, no blog post, no tweet. 

This is a significant result, yet both OpenAI and Anthropic chose to simply dump it online with no comment. I was listening to a Scott Aaronson interview this morning where he said this specific result would update him toward 'a solution to P ≠ NP by the AIs might really be around the corner.'
To me this is more evidence for my argument that both OpenAI and Anthropic are sitting on a dragon's hoard of scientific results they are not releasing to the public. The first massive 700+ paper OpenAI GitHub dump took five weeks for their model to generate. It's been seven weeks since then, and their internal model has continued to improve. They said they had it working on 4,000 problems. How many have been solved in the last seven weeks? Based on the last release, 1,000+ is not unreasonable.

I will quote OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki from the blog post 'Perplexity and Intelligence,' posted 48 hours ago:

'We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we've long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal.'

There have also been, of late, multiple rumors about breakthroughs in cryptography that I have been reluctant to post about for obvious reasons. Specifically, there have been rumors of an encryption breakthrough at Anthropic. What I personally took from the big OpenAI math release was that all encryption will be cracked much sooner than people are expecting, and that the rate of scientific discoveries will continually increase as we continue to scale up. No, not will increase, *has increased*. At both labs. We just don't know about it yet. Because unless you work at those labs, the current frontier is completely invisible. But it won't stay that way forever. Or to put it another way: prepare yourself for revelations.

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.
